newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel offers summit with U.S., PLO to forge deal.
newsitem.headline: Israel offers summit with U.S., PLO to forge deal.

text.p: Israel's Benjamin Netanyahu, facing world criticism and West Bank clashes, offered on Friday to meet U.S. and Palestinian leaders for three-way Camp David-style talks if necessary to forge a final peace deal.

Yet even as the prime minister spoke on Germany's ARD television, Israeli troops in Hebron battled 400 Palestinian stone-throwers on a 16th consecutive day of West Bank rage over a Jewish settlement in Arab East Jerusalem.

"As soon as violence against us stops, we can clear up all outstanding questions in six months," Netanyahu said in the interview from Israel ahead of a crisis meeting with President Bill Clinton at the White House on Monday.

"If we don't manage that within that time, then Arafat, President Clinton and I can try to settle the Israeli- Palestinian dispute in a sort of Camp David summit," he said, referring to Palestinian President Yasser Arafat.

Thirteen days of intensive U.S.-Israeli-Egyptian talks at the U.S. presidential retreat in Camp David near Washington in 1978 paved the way for Israel's 1979 peace treaty with Egypt, its first with an Arab state.

Washington, the main sponsor of interim peace deals signed by Israel and the Palestinians since 1993, has so far described as premature reports in the U.S. and Israeli news media of a possible Camp David summit to clinch an Israeli-PLO deal.
"We haven't decided on anything yet. We're at the sifting-through stage," one U.S. official said this week.

On Thursday night Netanyahu signalled no end to a Jewish settlement on a hill called Har Homa in Hebrew and Jabal Abu Ghneim in Arabic. Clashes have flared daily since Israel broke ground on the site for 6,500 homes for Jews.
Israel regards Jerusalem as its eternal capital. The PLO wants East Jerusalem as capital of a Palestinian state.

Palestinians have not ruled out a Camp David-style summit but doubt Washington's ability to be an honest broker after it twice vetoed U.N. Security Council resolutions to censure Israel over the Jerusalem settlement.

Chief Palestinian negotiator Saeb Erekat said Palestinians were considering sending peace envoys to the United States but he said: "Although we want to preserve the peace process, I am not very optimistic."
Palestinians balked at Netanyahu's offer to skip over an existing deal on phased Israeli West Bank troop pullbacks and dive into go-for-broke "final status" peace talks.
"This is a black joke," negotiator Hassan Asfour said.

Former Israeli prime minister Shimon Peres, the Nobel peace laureate narrowly defeated by Netanyahu last May, voiced similar scepticism that his right-wing rival could achieve a swift end to a century of conflict.
"In the run-up to the elections Mr Netanyahu and others accused me of going too fast. Suddenly they've...started discussing a swift pace," Peres told Israeli army radio.

"The problem in my view isn't the pace. The problem in my view is where do they want to go? If they're going to say 'no' to the Palestinians on everything, why hurry? We'll reach a confrontation," Peres said.
Israel demands Arafat crack down on "terrorism" as a condition for restarting talks. The PLO demands Israel halt work on the settlement.

While talks have stalled, Israeli troops have shot dead three Palestinians in the unrest. A suicide bomber killed three Israelis in a Tel Aviv blast. Two Palestinians died in botched suicide attacks in Gaza.
